title: app chart values
description: Helm validates the merged values against this schema on lint, template, install and upgrade. Every object closes with additionalProperties:false or a typed additionalProperties, so an unknown key is a failed release rather than a setting that silently did nothing.

environment.description: Which environment this release is. Mirrors the EksStack instances in aws/cdk/bin/app.ts; adding a third means adding it here, adding values-<env>.yaml, and adding it to ENVIRONMENTS in tools/audit-helm-values.ts.

nameOverride.description: Replaces the chart-name half of generated resource names.

replicaCount.description: Desired pods when autoscaling.enabled is false. With the HPA on, the Deployment renders no replicas field at all and this value does not reach the cluster — npm run audit:helm keeps it inside the HPA's range so that turning autoscaling off is not also a change of capacity.

autoscaling.description: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler. Scales pods against CPU utilization; the Cluster Autoscaler in EksStack scales the nodes underneath. docs/autoscaling.md derives every threshold here.

minReplicas.description: The HPA's floor, and the number the PodDisruptionBudget is checked against when autoscaling is on. Kubernetes requires at least 1 without the HPAScaleToZero feature gate, which EKS does not enable.

maxReplicas.description: The ceiling. Must exceed minReplicas — checked by npm run audit:helm, since JSON Schema cannot compare two properties — and maxReplicas × resources.requests.cpu must fit what the Cluster Autoscaler's maximum node count can supply, or the HPA scales into Pending pods.

targetCPUUtilizationPercentage.description: Percentage of the CPU request, not of the limit or the node. The gap between this and the service's latency knee is the headroom that covers the ~90s between load arriving and a new pod serving.

targetMemoryUtilizationPercentage.description: Optional, and usually wrong when requests.memory equals limits.memory: a runtime that holds freed pages sits near its target permanently, so the HPA scales up and never back down. Set it only for a service whose memory tracks concurrency.

allOf.description: A scale-down with no stabilization window removes pods on the first low sample and adds them back on the next, which turns ordinary traffic noise into a rollout. Kubernetes itself defaults to 300s; this chart's floor is 60s, deliberately lower than that default so a service with a genuinely short trough can opt into a faster one without editing the schema.

tag.description: Immutable image tag. Moving tags are rejected: with one, the running image depends on when a pod last restarted, so two pods in a ReplicaSet can serve different code and a rollback has no fixed target to return to.

imagePullSecrets.description: Names of image pull secrets. Empty for ECR, which is authorised through the node role.

name.description: Defaults to the release fullname when empty. Must be set when create is false.

annotations.description: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn goes here, bound to a role whose trust policy names this namespace and service account.

podSecurityContext.description: Pod-level security context: the identity every container runs as. Fields that belong to the container context (capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation) are not valid here and are rejected rather than silently ignored. The constants below are the restricted Pod Security Standard's non-negotiable half — a chart that lets an environment file override them cannot be admitted to a namespace enforcing that standard. fsGroup is what owns the writableVolumes emptyDirs: without it they are root-owned, and a read-only root filesystem then leaves the container with nowhere to write at all.

runAsNonRoot.description: Fixed true. This is the assertion the kubelet checks before starting the container, and it is the only one that catches an image whose USER is root when the manifest forgot to say otherwise.

securityContext.description: Container-level security context: what the process may do once it is running. Every constraint here is a const rather than a default, because an environment file relaxing one is not tuning a setting — it is opting out of the posture the chart is built on, and it should fail to render rather than deploy.

allowPrivilegeEscalation.description: Fixed false. Blocks setuid binaries and file capabilities from raising privileges mid-process, which is the step most container escapes take after gaining code execution as an unprivileged user.

privileged.description: Fixed false. A privileged container has the host's devices and every capability; nothing this chart deploys is an agent or a CSI driver.

readOnlyRootFilesystem.description: Fixed true. Scratch space comes from writableVolumes instead — see the note there on why an unbounded emptyDir is refused.

drop.description: Must contain ALL. Enumerating the capabilities to drop instead means revisiting the list whenever a runtime changes its default set, and nothing announces when that happens.

add.description: Capabilities granted back after the drop. npm run audit:helm allows NET_BIND_SERVICE and nothing else, and only when containerPort is below 1024 — a capability that is granted and unused is a capability nobody will remember was granted.

writableVolumes.description: emptyDir volumes mounted read-write into the container, which is how a read-only root filesystem stays workable. Mounted at the same paths in every environment: scratch space that exists only in staging is scratch space production discovers it needs during an incident. sizeLimit is required — an emptyDir with no limit draws on the node's shared ephemeral storage, so a service that leaks temporary files evicts its neighbours before itself and the eviction names the node rather than the cause.

name.description: Volume name, and a DNS label because it becomes one in the pod spec.

mountPath.description: Absolute, with no trailing slash and no empty segment. Bare `/` is unrepresentable here on purpose: mounting a writable volume over the root would undo readOnlyRootFilesystem while leaving it set to true.

type.description: ClusterIP unless something outside the cluster reaches this Service directly. The Ingress terminates at this Service and reaches it from inside the cluster, so it needs nothing wider.

ingress.description: The public entry point: one Ingress, always TLS, with the certificate issued and renewed by cert-manager and the DNS record published by external-dns. See docs/ingress.md.

then.description: An enabled Ingress with no host serves nothing and issues no certificate: the rule list is empty, spec.tls carries no SAN, and cert-manager's ingress-shim has nothing to create a Certificate for. The object is still valid Kubernetes, so only this catches it.

className.description: The IngressClass the controller registers. Not the deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation, which ingress-nginx 1.0 stopped honouring: an Ingress naming no class is admitted, listed, and served by nothing.

hosts.description: Every hostname served, and every SAN on the issued certificate — spec.tls carries the same list, so one certificate covers all of them.

path.description: Must start with a slash. Kubernetes rejects a path that does not, but only at apply time — which for a GitOps release is after the merge.

pathType.description: Prefix unless there is a reason. ImplementationSpecific hands matching to the controller, and ingress-nginx reads those paths as regular expressions when use-regex is on, so a dot silently becomes a wildcard.

tls.description: Not optional, and there is no tls.enabled. An Ingress without spec.tls makes the cert-manager annotation a no-op — ingress-shim reads the TLS hosts, not the rule hosts — and reports nothing at all.

clusterIssuer.description: The ClusterIssuer name. It differs per environment because the staging cluster issues from Let's Encrypt's staging ACME endpoint; npm run audit:helm checks the two agree.

renewBefore.description: A Go duration ending in h, m or s. cert-manager rejects a bare number, and rejects the d suffix that everybody writes first.

secretName.description: Defaults to <fullname>-tls. Two releases naming one Secret produce two Certificates that overwrite each other's key pair at renewal.

resources.description: Required, not optional. No requests means BestEffort scheduling and first eviction under node pressure; no memory limit means one leaking container can evict every other pod on the node.

limits.description: A memory limit is required and a CPU limit is not: memory is incompressible, while a CPU limit adds CFS throttling latency to a service that is not otherwise short of CPU.

config.description: Rendered into a ConfigMap and injected with envFrom. Values must be strings: ConfigMap data is string-valued, so an unquoted 8080 is rejected by the API server at apply time — here it is rejected at lint time instead.

extraEnv.description: Environment variables that are not plain configuration — a downward-API field, or one that must be ordered after envFrom.

podDisruptionBudget.description: What makes a node drain wait for a replacement pod instead of taking the last healthy replica.

minAvailable.description: A count, not a percentage, so its meaning does not change when replicaCount does. Must stay below replicaCount — a budget equal to the replica count blocks every drain forever, which stops cluster upgrades rather than protecting the service. Checked against replicaCount by npm run audit:helm, which the schema cannot do because JSON Schema cannot compare two properties.

strategy.description: RollingUpdate parameters. maxUnavailable 0 keeps capacity flat through a rollout, at the cost of one extra pod for its duration.

terminationGracePeriodSeconds.description: Must exceed the longest in-flight request, or every deploy truncates responses.

networkPolicy.description: Default-deny NetworkPolicy plus an explicit allowlist. Kubernetes has no built-in policy controller, so these objects are stored and ignored on a CNI that does not implement policy — on EKS that is the VPC CNI's network policy agent, which EksStack enables through the add-on's configurationValues. See docs/network-policies.md.

enabled.description: Off is for a cluster whose CNI cannot enforce policy, not for unblocking a service. npm run audit:helm fails on a values file that disables it, so the quick fix is not also the silent one.

dns.description: Egress to cluster DNS, held apart from the egress allowlist because it is not a policy decision: without it a default-deny egress policy drops every name lookup, and the symptom is a resolver timeout rather than anything that names the network.

ingress.description: Who may open a connection to these pods. Empty denies everything, which is the default. Ports here are matched against the pod's containerPort, not the Service port — kube-proxy rewrites the destination before policy is evaluated.

egress.description: Where these pods may open a connection to. Empty denies everything except cluster DNS, which is rendered from networkPolicy.dns.

hpaScalingRules.description: One direction of an HPA's behavior. The two policy kinds are named keys rather than the API's array, because Helm replaces arrays wholesale: an environment file changing one policy in a list would have to restate the others, and the one it forgot would vanish.

stabilizationWindowSeconds.description: The window the HPA takes its most conservative recommendation from. Absent is not the same as 0: absent falls back to the API default, which is 0 for scale-up and 300 for scale-down. The chart always renders it, so it is required here.

selectPolicy.description: Which policy wins when both percent and pods are set: Max takes the larger change, Min the smaller, Disabled blocks movement in this direction entirely. Irrelevant with a single policy.

hpaScalingPolicy.description: How much the HPA may move the replica count in one period, in percent of the current count or in absolute pods.

unprivilegedId.description: A UID or GID that is not root. 0 is excluded here rather than left to runAsNonRoot, because the two disagreeing — runAsNonRoot: true with runAsUser: 0 — is a manifest the API server accepts and the kubelet then refuses to start, so the failure lands as a CreateContainerConfigError on the cluster instead of on the person editing the values file. The ceiling is the 16-bit range: a UID above it falls outside what most base images' /etc/passwd and the default userns mapping cover, and an unmapped UID appears as `nobody`.

capability.description: A Linux capability as Kubernetes names it — without the CAP_ prefix, which the runtime adds. `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` here becomes `CAP_CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, which no runtime grants and none reports as an error, so the prefix is rejected rather than passed through.

seccompProfile.description: The seccomp filter applied to every container in the pod. Absent is not neutral — it means Unconfined, which is the weakest of the three settings and the Kubernetes default, so Unconfined is not offered as a value here.

localhostProfile.description: Path of a profile relative to the kubelet's seccomp root, for type: Localhost.

oneOf.description: RuntimeDefault takes no profile path. One supplied alongside it is silently ignored by the kubelet, which reads as a custom profile being enforced when the runtime's default is.
Localhost without a profile path is a pod the API server rejects outright.

networkPolicyRule.description: One allowlist entry, which becomes exactly one element of a NetworkPolicy from/to list. One element, so namespaceLabels and podLabels are ANDed: the same two selectors split across two elements would mean 'either', and the two forms are one character apart in YAML. Allowing two sources means writing two entries.

anyOf.description: A peer with neither an ipBlock nor a selector is rejected by the API server, and would read as 'everything' to anyone who got it past that.

not.description: ipBlock and the selectors are mutually exclusive within one peer. The API server accepts an entry carrying both and what a CNI then does with it is not defined by anything worth relying on, so it is refused here.

except.description: An except list without a cidr has nothing to subtract from.

name.description: Not rendered — a NetworkPolicy rule has no name field. It is what review and an audit failure can refer to, instead of a list index.

podLabels.description: Without namespaceLabels alongside it, this matches those pods in the release's own namespace — not in every namespace, which is how it reads.

except.description: Ranges subtracted from cidr. Each must fall inside it, which the API server checks and this schema cannot.

ports.description: Required, and non-empty. A from/to with no ports allows every port from that peer — an allowlist entry that names a source and then does not limit what it may do.

networkPolicyEgressRule.description: An allowlist entry in the egress direction. Identical to an ingress entry except that its ports must be numbers, refined here the way scaleDown refines hpaScalingRules above.

allOf.description: A named port is resolved against the containers of the pod the traffic is going to. On ingress that is this chart's pod, so `port: http` is exact. On egress it is somebody else's pod, where the name means whatever they called it — so it matches nothing the moment they call it something else, and there is no error anywhere when it stops matching.

port.description: A number, or the name of a container port on the destination pod. Ingress ports are matched against containerPort and not against service.port: the destination is rewritten by kube-proxy before policy is evaluated, so an entry naming the Service's port matches nothing and the connection is dropped.

protocol.description: Defaults to TCP in Kubernetes as well; the chart renders it explicitly, because an omitted protocol reads as 'any' and is not.

matchLabels.description: Labels a peer selector matches on. At least one: an empty matchLabels is a selector that matches everything, so `namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {}}` is every namespace in the cluster — an allowlist entry that reads as narrow and is the widest one there is.

hostname.description: A DNS name, lower-case, at least two labels, and no scheme, port or path — `https://app.example.com` is the value everybody writes first, and the API server accepts it as a host that then matches no request. A leading `*.` is refused as well: a wildcard SAN can only be issued through a DNS-01 challenge on the apex, so it is a decision about the issuer rather than a longer hostname, and docs/ingress.md §6 has it.

cidr.description: An IPv4 CIDR block. IPv6 is not accepted because nothing this repository provisions is dual-stack, and a v6 range in an allowlist on a v4-only cluster is a rule that silently matches nothing.

cpuQuantity.description: Kubernetes CPU quantity: cores (1, 1.5) or millicores (500m).

memoryQuantity.description: Kubernetes memory quantity. Binary suffixes (Mi, Gi) are what the API server reports back, so using them keeps values and observed limits comparable.

countOrPercent.description: An absolute pod count or a percentage string, which is what the Deployment API accepts.

probe.description: An HTTP GET probe against the container's named http port.
